Overview
Clean air is fundamental to health. Compared to 15 years ago, when the previous edition
of these guidelines was published, there is now a much stronger body of evidence to
show how air pollution affects different aspects of health at even lower concentrations
than previously understood. But here’s what hasn’t changed: every year, exposure to
air pollution is still estimated to cause millions of deaths and the loss of healthy years
of life.
The burden of disease attributable to air pollution is now estimated to be on
a par with other major global health risks such as unhealthy diets and tobacco smoking.

WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines
22 September 2021 | Questions and answers
The updated WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines (AQGs) provide recommendations on air quality guideline levels as well as interim targets for six key air pollutants. They also offer qualitative statements on good practices for the management of certain types of particulate matter (PM), for example, black carbon/elemental carbon, ultrafine particles, and particles originating from sand and dust storms, for which there is insufficient quantitative evidence to derive AQG levels.
What are the WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines?
The updated WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines (AQGs) provide recommendations on air quality guideline levels as well as interim targets for six key air pollutants. They also offer qualitative statements on good practices for the management of certain types of particulate matter (PM), for example, black carbon/elemental carbon, ultrafine particles, and particles originating from sand and dust storms, for which there is insufficient quantitative evidence to derive AQG levels.

quotes.whole:
offer additional AQG levels, such as for peak season O₃ and 24-hour NO₂ and CO, as well as some new interim targets;
offer new good practice statements on the management of certain types of PM (i.e. black carbon/elemental carbon, ultrafine particles, and particles originating from sand and dust storms).
What is air pollution and where are these pollutants found in daily life?
Air pollution is the contamination of the air we breathe, indoors or outdoors, by any chemical, physical or biological agent that is potentially threatening to human and ecosystem health. The pollutants with the most robust evidence for public health
concern include particulate matter (PM), ozone (O₃), nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) and sulfur dioxide (SO₂) and carbon monoxide (CO). The health risks associated with PM smaller than or equal to 2.5 microns (µm) in diameter (PM₂.₅) are of particular
public health relevance. PM₂.₅ and PM₁₀ are capable of penetrating deep into the lungs and PM₂.₅ can even enter the bloodstream, primarily resulting in cardiovascular and respiratory impacts. In 2013, outdoor air pollution and PM were classified as
carcinogenic by WHO’s International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC).

Other Titles







Abstract

These WHO global air quality guidelines present updated evidence-based recommendations to protect public health from the adverse effects of air pollution. Developed in response to substantial advances in scientific evidence since the 2005 guidelines, they provide quantitative air quality guideline (AQG) levels for particulate matter (PM₂.₅ and PM₁₀), ozone, nitrogen dioxide, sulfur dioxide and carbon monoxide, together with interim targets to support progressive reductions in exposure where guideline levels cannot be achieved immediately. The recommendations are based on systematic reviews and rigorous evaluation of the evidence linking air pollution to adverse health outcomes and are intended to inform legislation, policy and air quality management worldwide.

The guidelines also include good practice statements for black carbon/elemental carbon, ultrafine particles, and particles from sand and dust storms, for which evidence indicates health risks but remains insufficient to establish quantitative guideline levels. Applicable to both outdoor and indoor environments, they serve as a global reference for policy-makers, technical experts, public authorities, researchers and civil society. The document outlines principles for dissemination, implementation, monitoring and evaluation, emphasizes the role of the health sector and intersectoral collaboration, and identifies research priorities to strengthen future evidence and support continued improvements in air quality and population health.

of life.

# WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines (2021) — recommended AQG levels

## Answers

| Item | Pollutant / metric | Recommended AQG level (2021) |
|---|---|---|
| (a) | Sulfur dioxide (SO₂), **24-hour mean** | **40 µg/m³** |
| (b) | Nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), **annual mean** | **10 µg/m³** |

Both are the *air quality guideline (AQG) level* — the health-based recommended level — not the interim targets. Units are µg/m³ as requested (mass concentration at reference conditions of 25 °C and 101.325 kPa, the basis WHO uses for these guideline tables).

## Metric definitions as WHO states them

- **24-hour mean (SO₂):** the arithmetic mean of the hourly concentrations over a calendar day; WHO's 24-hour guideline values are conventionally assessed as the 99th percentile of daily 24-hour means over a year (i.e. permitting 3–4 exceedance days per year) when used for compliance purposes. The guideline value itself is the 24-hour mean concentration.
- **Annual mean (NO₂):** the arithmetic mean of all valid hourly (or shorter-interval) measurements across a calendar year (WHO allows a year to be represented by a continuous period of at least 6 months, or by non-continuous measurements spread over the year).

## Full guideline ladders from the same source (for context and cross-checking)

SO₂ — 24-hour mean

| Level | Value (µg/m³) |
|---|---|
| Interim target 1 | 125 |
| Interim target 2 | 50 |
| **AQG level** | **40** |

What is REACH?
What is REACH?
What is REACH?
REACH is the EU's comprehensive chemicals regulation and the cornerstone of EU chemical regulations. For supply chain teams, the primary obligation is managing Substances of Very High Concern (SVHCs)—chemicals posing serious risks due to carcinogenic, mutagenic, persistent, bioaccumulative, or endocrine-disrupting properties.
The Candidate List contains 253 SVHCs as of February 2026. ECHA has shifted toward up to three Candidate List updates per year—January, June, and November. Companies placing articles on the EU market containing SVHCs above 0.1% w/w must communicate this down the supply chain, respond to consumer requests within 45 days, and submit SCIP database notifications.
REACH compliance requires substance-level data—CAS numbers and weight percentages—from every supplier. When new SVHCs are added, your entire portfolio requires reassessment.

verdict.summary:
# Retailer's duty to answer a consumer SVHC question — REACH Article 33(2)

## 0. Answers

| # | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Above what concentration in the article does the duty to answer arise? | **0.1 % w/w** (weight by weight) of the substance in the article — i.e. 1 000 mg/kg = 1 000 ppm = 1 g/kg |
| 2 | Within how many days must the retailer answer? | **45 days** from receipt of the request (calendar days) |
| 3 | May the retailer charge for the answer? | **No** — the information must be provided free of charge |

All three come from the same operative sentence-pair of Article 33(2) REACH, so they stand or fall together.

---

## 1. Legal basis (operative text)

Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 (REACH), Article 33 — *Duty to communicate information on substances in articles*:

> **1.** Any supplier of an article containing a substance meeting the criteria in Article 57 and identified in accordance with Article 59(1) in a concentration above 0,1 % weight by weight (w/w) shall provide the recipient of the article with sufficient information, available to the supplier, to allow safe use of the article including, as a minimum, the name of that substance.
>
> **2.** On request by a consumer any supplier of an article containing a substance meeting the criteria in Article 57 and identified in accordance with Article 59(1) in a concentration above 0,1 % weight by weight (w/w) shall provide the consumer with sufficient information, available to the supplier, to allow safe use of the article including, as a minimum, the name of that substance.
>
> The relevant information shall be provided, **free of charge**, **within 45 days** of receipt of the request.

Source: https://www.legislation.gov.uk/eur/2006/1907/article/33 (and the 12/10/2008 consolidated version at the same site); text substituted by the Corrigendum to Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 (OJ L 396, 30.12.2006).

**Why the retailer is caught.** Article 33(2) is addressed to "any supplier of an article". "Supplier" is defined in Article 3(32) REACH as any manufacturer, importer, downstream user **or distributor** placing a substance, mixture or article on the market. A retailer that places the article on the market is therefore a supplier for Article 33(2) purposes and owes the duty directly to the consumer — it does not sit only with the manufacturer or importer. "Consumer" is defined in Article 3(34) as a natural or legal person acting outside its trade, business or profession.

**Condition precedent.** The duty is triggered only where **both** limbs are met: (i) the substance meets the Article 57 criteria and is on the Candidate List adopted under Article 59(1); and (ii) it is present in the article **above 0.1 % w/w**. If either limb fails, no Article 33(2) duty arises for that substance.

---

## 2. Ask 1 — the concentration threshold in detail

### 2.1 The figure

**0.1 % w/w** of the Candidate List substance in the article. Conversions, all identical:

- 0.1 % w/w = **1 000 mg/kg**
- = **1 000 ppm**
- = **1 g/kg**
- = 0.001 mass fraction

### 2.2 What the concentration is measured against

The denominator is the mass of the **article** — the object as placed on the market, given the shape, surface or design that determines its function more than its chemical composition (Article 3(3) REACH). The numerator is the mass of the Candidate List substance present in that article. So:

```
concentration (% w/w) = (mass of SVHC in the article / mass of the article) x 100
```

### 2.3 Per article, not per complex object

Where the product is a **complex object** made of several articles (a bicycle, a chair, a jacket with a zip), the threshold is applied **article by article**, not to the assembled product as a whole. This is the effect of CJEU Case C-106/14 (*FCD and FMB*, judgment of 10 September 2015), which held that Article 33 applies where an article incorporated into a complex product contains an SVHC above 0.1 % w/w of **that article**. The consequence is counter-intuitive and must be applied literally: a substance can be far below 0.1 % of the finished product and still trigger the duty.

**Worked example (complex object).** A bicycle weighs 12 kg. A handlebar grip is a separate article weighing 200 g and contains 0.5 g of an SVHC.

- Per governing basis (the grip, which is the article): 0.5 g / 200 g = **0.25 % w/w → above 0.1 % → duty arises.**
- For illustration only, *not* the governing basis: 0.5 g / 12 000 g = 0.00417 % w/w of the whole bicycle.

The retailer must answer, even though the whole-product figure looks negligible.

### 2.4 Simple worked example (single article)

An article weighs 2.5 kg (2 500 g).

| SVHC present | Calculation | Result | Duty? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 g | 3 / 2 500 x 100 = 0.12 % | above 0.1 % | **Yes** |
| 2 g | 2 / 2 500 x 100 = 0.08 % | below 0.1 % | No (for that substance) |

### 2.5 Points that do **not** change the 0.1 % figure

- **No tonnage threshold.** Article 33 has no volume or tonnage condition. The >1 tonne per producer/importer per year condition belongs to the **separate** Article 7(2) notification duty to ECHA; it does not qualify Article 33 and must not be imported into it.
- **No intentionality requirement.** The threshold is about presence, not function. A substance present as a residual impurity, contaminant or legacy component above 0.1 % w/w triggers the duty just as an intentionally added substance does.
- **The threshold itself has not been amended.** What changes over time is the **content of the Candidate List** (ECHA updates it, currently up to three times a year — January, June, November; 253 entries as of February 2026). A substance not on the list on the date of the request creates no Article 33(2) duty, however hazardous. The 0.1 % figure is fixed in the Article.
- **Date of placing on the market** is largely irrelevant to Article 33(2): the duty attaches to the article the supplier is supplying and to the list as it stands. Do not run the analysis against a historical list unless the enforcement authority's practice in the relevant Member State requires it.

---

## 3. Ask 2 — the 45-day deadline in detail

- **Clock starts** on **receipt of the request** by the supplier — i.e. by the retailer. Not the date the consumer sent it, and not the date the retailer's own supplier was asked.
- **45 days** — the Article says "days", not "working days". Read as **calendar days**. There is no provision converting them to working days and no mechanism in the text for suspending or extending the period.
- **The retailer's internal information chain does not extend the deadline.** The duty is qualified by "available to the supplier" (see §4), not by a grace period. If the retailer must ask its upstream supplier, that must be done inside the 45 days. Enforcement authorities do not accept "we were waiting for our supplier" as a defence to a late answer.
- **45 days is a maximum, not a minimum.** Answering on day 3 is compliant. Never write "the retailer has 45 days to decide whether to answer" — the answer is mandatory within the window.
- **What must be in the answer.** "Sufficient information, available to the supplier, to allow safe use of the article", including **as a minimum the name of the substance**. Practically: substance name (and ideally the Candidate List entry date and, where held, CAS/EC number), the fact of presence above 0.1 % w/w, and the safe-use information the retailer holds (e.g. "do not allow children to mouth the item", "wash hands after handling", handling/storage/disposal instructions received from the supplier).
- **"Available to the supplier" is a scope limit on content, not a defence to silence.** The retailer must give what it has or can reasonably obtain. It cannot be required to commission new testing, but it also cannot refuse to answer.

---

## 4. Ask 3 — no fee, in detail

The third subparagraph of Article 33(2) is unambiguous: "The relevant information shall be provided, **free of charge**, within 45 days of receipt of the request."

Therefore the retailer **may not** charge the consumer, and in particular may not charge:

- a handling, administration or research fee;
- a postage or copying fee for a paper response;
- a fee for time spent querying its own supplier;
- a fee conditional on the consumer buying something, or a fee refundable on purchase.

An answer given only on payment is not an answer for Article 33(2) purposes; conditioning the response on payment is itself a breach, and it will also usually cause the 45-day deadline to be missed while the fee discussion runs.

---

## 5. Procedure the retailer should follow

**Step 1 — log the request.** Record date of receipt (this starts the 45-day clock), the consumer, the product and the specific substance asked about. Set an internal deadline at **day 35** to leave 10 days of margin.

**Step 2 — identify the article(s).** If the product is a complex object, decompose it into its constituent articles. The analysis in Step 3 runs per article.

**Step 3 — check the substance against the Candidate List as at the date of the request.** If the substance is not on the list, there is no Article 33(2) duty for it — but still reply politely explaining that, because a non-answer looks like a breach to an enforcement authority and to the consumer.

**Step 4 — establish concentration per article.** Use the bill of materials / full material declaration from the upstream supplier. Compare against **0.1 % w/w**. Where a supplier declares only "contains" without a percentage, escalate to that supplier immediately and in writing, citing the 45-day deadline.

**Step 5 — respond within 45 days, free of charge, in one of three forms:**

- **Above 0.1 % w/w** → give the substance name (minimum) plus the safe-use information held. Template A below.
- **At or below 0.1 % w/w** → state that, on the information available, the substance is not present above 0.1 % w/w in the article. Template B below. (Strictly the Article 33(2) duty is not engaged, but a clear negative answer is the correct risk position.)
- **Genuinely unknown after reasonable enquiry** → say so expressly, say what was done to find out, give whatever is known (including the substance name if presence is known but concentration is not), and give safe-use advice on a precautionary basis. Template C below. Silence is not an option; an unsupported "we don't hold that data" is the highest-risk answer in enforcement practice.

**Step 6 — keep the record.** Retain the request, the date stamp, the supplier declarations relied on, and the answer sent. This is the evidence that decides any enforcement file.

### Template A — above threshold

> Dear [consumer],
> Thank you for your request of [date] concerning [product]. We received it on [date].
> This product contains [substance name], a substance of very high concern included on the ECHA Candidate List (entry added [date]), in a concentration above 0.1 % weight by weight in the following article: [article / component].
> Safe use information: [handling, storage, disposal, restrictions on use, e.g. keep out of reach of children / do not mouth / wash hands after contact / dispose of as [route]].
> This information is provided free of charge under Article 33(2) of Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 (REACH).
> Yours, [retailer]

### Template B — at or below threshold

> Dear [consumer],
> Thank you for your request of [date] concerning [product], received on [date].
> On the basis of the information available to us from our suppliers, [substance name] is not present in [product] in a concentration above 0.1 % weight by weight in any article of the product. Article 33(2) of Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 therefore does not require further information for this substance.
> We provide this answer free of charge. If you have further questions, please contact [details].

### Template C — information not available

> Dear [consumer],
> Thank you for your request of [date] concerning [product], received on [date].
> [Substance name] is on the ECHA Candidate List. We have asked our supplier for the concentration data for [article] on [date] and [state outcome]. The concentration data is not currently available to us. [If presence is known but concentration is not: The substance is present in [article]; the exact concentration has not been declared to us.]
> On a precautionary basis we recommend: [safe-use advice].
> We will send you the confirmed concentration information if and when it becomes available to us. This information is provided free of charge under Article 33(2) of Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 (REACH).

---

## 6. Common errors to avoid (each one is a live enforcement finding)

1. **Applying 0.1 % to the whole complex product** instead of to each constituent article (contradicts C-106/14).
2. **Importing the 1 t/a threshold from Article 7(2)** into the Article 33 analysis. Article 33 has no tonnage condition.
3. **Treating 45 days as extendable** because the retailer is waiting on its own supplier. It is not.
4. **Charging any fee**, including postage or an "administrative" charge.
5. **Answering only "the product complies with REACH"** — that is not the information Article 33(2) requires; the substance name is the stated minimum.
6. **Not answering at all** because the answer is negative. A negative answer is still an answer and should be sent within the window.
7. **Confusing SCIP with the consumer route.** SCIP notification to ECHA's database (Waste Framework Directive 2008/98/EC, Article 9(1)(i), required since 5 January 2021) is a separate obligation on suppliers of articles; it does **not** discharge the Article 33(2) duty and does not give the consumer an answer. The retailer must still reply within 45 days, free of charge.

---

## 7. Enforcement and consequence

Article 33 is a REACH obligation; Member States set penalties under Article 126 REACH, which must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive. National regimes vary widely (administrative fines, injunctions, in some Member States criminal exposure for persistent non-compliance). The practical exposure for a retailer is (a) the finding of a refusal or a late answer, and (b) the finding that a fee was charged — both are recorded breaches independent of whether the substance was in fact above 0.1 % w/w.

---

## 8. Scope limits — when this answer would not apply

This answer is stated for the **EU REACH regime as currently in force**, applied to a **consumer request about an article**, where the substance is on the Candidate List at the date of the request. It would **not** be the right answer if:

- **The product is a mixture/preparation, not an article.** Then Article 33 does not apply at all; the relevant routes are the safety data sheet and information duties of Articles 31 and 32, and the consumer's route is generally via the supplier's SDS or the point of sale, not Article 33.
- **The question is asked by a professional/industrial recipient rather than a consumer.** Then Article 33(1) applies — same 0.1 % threshold, but the information is provided **at the time of supply**, not on a 45-day request clock, and the "free of charge" sentence is drafted around the consumer request.
- **A Member State's enforcement practice reads "available to the supplier" more strictly.** Some authorities expect the retailer to have contractual data-flow from its suppliers and treat "we don't know" as non-compliance. The 0.1 % / 45 days / free of charge answers are unchanged; only the standard applied to the content of the answer shifts.
- **The question is asked about the UK regime.** The GB version of REACH (as retained) is published separately on legislation.gov.uk and, while Article 33 is textually the same, the GB Candidate List is maintained separately by HSE/Defra and diverges from the EU list.

None of these variants changes the three answers given: **0.1 % w/w; 45 days; free of charge.**

verdict.summary:
ROHS ANNEX II (DIRECTIVE 2011/65/EU) — CONSOLIDATED READING

BASIS OF ANSWER (version relied on)
The answer is given against Annex II of Directive 2011/65/EU as substituted by Commission Delegated Directive (EU) 2015/863 of 31 March 2015 (OJ L 137, 4.6.2015), which is the version carried in the current consolidated text on EUR-Lex (the EUR-Lex ELI page for the act shows a current consolidated version dated 01/07/2026) and mirrored in the revised versions published on legislation.gov.uk (latest revision listed: 01/09/2020; no amendments applied there after IP completion day, 31 December 2020). This matters for the count: the original 2011 recast Annex II contained only six substances and no phthalates at all; the 2015/863 substitution added four phthalates and is the operative consolidated text. All three answers below are read from that substituted Annex II.

---

1. NUMBER OF RESTRICTED SUBSTANCES: 10

Annex II ('Restricted substances referred to in Article 4(1) and maximum concentration values tolerated by weight in homogeneous materials'), as substituted by Delegated Directive (EU) 2015/863, lists ten entries:

| # | Restricted substance | Maximum concentration (by weight in homogeneous materials) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Lead | 0,1 % |
| 2 | Mercury | 0,1 % |
| 3 | Cadmium | 0,01 % |
| 4 | Hexavalent chromium | 0,1 % |
| 5 | Polybrominated biphenyls (PBB) | 0,1 % |
| 6 | Polybrominated diphenyl ethers (PBDE) | 0,1 % |
| 7 | Bis(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP) | 0,1 % |
| 8 | Butyl benzyl phthalate (BBP) | 0,1 % |
| 9 | Dibutyl phthalate (DBP) | 0,1 % |
| 10 | Diisobutyl phthalate (DIBP) | 0,1 % |

Count check: 4 metals + 2 brominated flame retardants + 4 phthalates = 10. Nine entries carry 0,1 %; exactly one carries 0,01 %.

---

2. THE SUBSTANCE WITH A MAXIMUM CONCENTRATION OF 0,01 % BY WEIGHT IN HOMOGENEOUS MATERIALS: CADMIUM

Cadmium is the only Annex II entry with a 0,01 % limit. All other nine entries (lead, mercury, hexavalent chromium, PBB, PBDE, DEHP, BBP, DBP, DIBP) are set at 0,1 %. The limit is expressed, as the Annex II heading states, by weight in homogeneous materials — i.e. it is assessed per homogeneous material, not per component or per whole appliance (Article 4(2) and the Commission's detailed rules on maximum concentration values, including surface coatings).

Note on decimal notation: the Directive uses the comma decimal separator ('0,01 %'), equivalent to 0.01 % w/w = 100 mg/kg (100 ppm) for cadmium; '0,1 %' = 0.1 % w/w = 1 000 mg/kg (1 000 ppm) for the other nine.

---

3. DATE FROM WHICH DEHP, BBP, DBP AND DIBP ARE RESTRICTED IN MEDICAL DEVICES: 22 JULY 2021

The Annex II text itself carries the application rule for the four phthalates:

  'The restriction of DEHP, BBP, DBP and DIBP shall apply to medical devices, including in vitro medical devices, and monitoring and control instruments, including industrial monitoring and control instruments, from 22 July 2021.'

So:
- General EEE (categories 1–7, 10, 11): the four phthalates apply from 22 July 2019.
- Medical devices, including in vitro medical devices (Annex I category 8), and monitoring and control instruments, including industrial monitoring and control instruments (category 9): 22 July 2021.

The same Annex II text contains the associated spare-parts carve-out, which does not change the date but limits its reach: the restriction does not apply to cables or spare parts for the repair, reuse, updating of functionalities or upgrading of capacity of EEE placed on the market before 22 July 2019, and of medical devices (including IVD) and monitoring and control instruments (including industrial) placed on the market before 22 July 2021. In other words, 22 July 2021 is the date from which newly placed-on-market medical devices must comply, while pre-22 July 2021 units may still be repaired/upgraded with non-compliant cables and spare parts.

Separately, Annex II states that the restriction of DEHP, BBP and DBP does not apply to toys already restricted through entry 51 of Annex XVII to Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 — irrelevant to medical devices, noted only for completeness of the Annex II footnote.

---

SCOPE NOTES AND QUALIFICATIONS (for the downstream reader)

(a) Time sensitivity. 'Currently consolidated' is a moving target. The answers above hold for any consolidation incorporating Delegated Directive (EU) 2015/863 — i.e. any version from 2015 onward. A pre-2015 consolidation would give 6 substances and no phthalate dates; if the requester intended a pre-2015 text, answer 1 becomes 6 and answer 3 has no answer within Annex II. The count and the phthalate date are therefore tied to the 2015/863-substituted text.

(b) 'Medical devices' here means Annex I category 8 (medical devices, including in vitro medical devices) and, for the same date, category 9 (monitoring and control instruments, including industrial monitoring and control instruments). The Directive gives both the same 22 July 2021 date for the four phthalates.

(c) Exemptions. Annexes III and IV contain application-specific exemptions (with expiry dates that for categories 8 and 9 run to 21 July 2021 / 21 July 2023 for category 8 IVD / 21 July 2024 for category 9 industrial monitoring and control, for the entries shown in the fetched text, e.g. 7(c)-I and 7(c)-IV). Those exemptions concern the original six substances (lead in solders, lead in PZT ceramics, etc.), not the four phthalates, and do not move the 22 July 2021 phthalate date. Any exemption actually relied on for a specific medical device application must be checked separately in Annex III/IV; it does not alter the general answers above.

(d) Do not conflate with Article 4(3). The dates 22 July 2014 (medical devices and monitoring and control instruments), 22 July 2016 (IVD) and 22 July 2017 (industrial monitoring and control) in Article 4(3) are the phase-in dates for the six original substances, not for the phthalates.

(e) Source hierarchy. The authoritative text is the EUR-Lex consolidated version of Directive 2011/65/EU; the legislation.gov.uk revised text used here reproduces the same Annex II wording (including the 22 July 2021 phthalate date) and is a reliable cross-check, but for a formal compliance file cite the EUR-Lex consolidation with its date and Delegated Directive (EU) 2015/863 as the amending act.

---

ANSWER SUMMARY
1. Restricted substances in Annex II (consolidated, post-2015/863): 10.
2. Substance with a 0,01 % by weight in homogeneous materials limit: Cadmium (all others 0,1 %).
3. Date from which DEHP, BBP, DBP and DIBP are restricted in medical devices (incl. IVD) and monitoring and control instruments: 22 July 2021 (general EEE date being 22 July 2019; pre-22 July 2021 devices retain the cables/spare-parts carve-out).

verdict.summary:
Applicable basis: IAEA Safety Standards Series No. SSR-6, Regulations for the Safe Transport of Radioactive Material, current edition (2018 edition, Rev. 1). The user should confirm that this is the edition in force for the particular shipment and that no stricter modal or national requirement applies.

TI determination
1. Maximum dose rate at 1 m from the external surfaces: 0.08 mSv/h.
2. Base TI = 0.08 × 100 = 8.0.
3. The article is a freight container, so SSR-6 Table 7 (multiplication factors for large-dimensional loads) applies. The largest cross-sectional area of the load is 3 m², which falls in the band 'greater than 1 m² and not exceeding 5 m²'. The Table 7 factor is 2.
4. Adjusted TI = 8.0 × 2 = 16.0.
5. TI is rounded up to the next tenth. 16.0 is already at the next tenth, so the assigned TI is 16.0 (dimensionless; shown on labels and shipping papers as 16.0).

TI limit check
For a freight container not under exclusive use, the SSR-6 Table 7 TI limit is 50. The assigned TI of 16.0 is below 50, with a margin of 34.0. Therefore the TI is within the applicable freight-container TI limit.

Result: TI = 16.0; within the non-exclusive-use freight-container TI limit of 50.

Caveat to record on the consignment file: SSR-6 also applies a TI cap of 10 to a package or overpack not under exclusive use. If the competent authority or modal regime treats this freight container solely as a package and applies the package cap rather than the freight-container cap, TI 16.0 would exceed that 10 cap and the consignment would not comply without exclusive use or additional shielding/re-stowage. The answer above applies the freight-container limit requested by the question.

Understanding Text Spacing |
How to Meet Text Spacing
(Level AA)
In content implemented using markup languages that support the following text style properties, no loss of content or functionality occurs by setting all of the following and by changing no other style property:
Line height (line spacing) to at least 1.5 times the font size;
Spacing following paragraphs to at least 2 times the font size;
Letter spacing (tracking) to at least 0.12 times the font size;
Word spacing to at least 0.16 times the font size.
Exception: Human languages and scripts that do not make use of one or more of these text style properties in written text can conform using only the properties that exist for that combination of language and script.
Note 1
Content is not required to use these text spacing values. The requirement is to ensure that when a user overrides the authored text spacing, content or functionality is not lost.

The majority of this material centers around touchscreen interactions, and suggests relatively large minimum sizes. In contrast, this criterion is scoped to all pointer input modalities – not just touch, but also mouse, trackpad, stylus and others. Requiring large, touch-optimized minimum sizes would not have been appropriate as a threshold for all pointer inputs. quotes.whole:
Note
When creating this success criterion, the Working Group reviewed existing research and guidelines. The majority of this material centers around touchscreen interactions, and suggests relatively large minimum sizes. In contrast, this criterion is scoped to all pointer input modalities – not just touch, but also mouse, trackpad, stylus and others. Requiring large, touch-optimized minimum sizes would not have been appropriate as a threshold for all pointer inputs. For this reason – after reviewing the average target size of various high-traffic sites – the Working Group settled on the smaller measure of 24 by 24 CSS pixels for the "(Minimum)" version of this criterion, while 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced) uses the larger 44 by 44 CSS pixel measure as its threshold size.
Exceptions
The requirement is for targets to be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels in size. There are five exceptions:
Spacing: Undersized targets (those less than 24 by 24 CSS pixels) are positioned so that if a 24 CSS pixel diameter circle is centered on the bounding box of each, the circles do not intersect another target or the circle for another undersized target.

quotes.whole:
The targets on a screen can have different purposes and uses, and this success criterion specifies how each is to be handled.
Equivalent targets: If there is more than one target on a screen that performs the same action, only one of the targets need to meet the target size of 44 by 44 CSS pixels.
Inline: The success criterion does not apply to inline targets in sentences or blocks of text. Content is often designed to reflow based on the screen width available. This is known as responsive design and makes it easier to read since you do not need to scroll both horizontally and vertically. In reflowed content, the targets can appear anywhere on a line and can change position based on the width of the available screen. Since targets can appear anywhere on the line, the size cannot be larger than the available text and spacing between the sentences or paragraphs, otherwise the targets could overlap. It is for this reason targets which are contained within one or more sentences are excluded from the target size requirements.
Note
If the target is the full sentence and the sentence is not in a block of text, then the target needs to be at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels.

verdict.summary:
# WCAG 2.2 pointer-target sizes — answers

## Answer table

| # | Question | Answer |
|---|----------|--------|
| 1 | Level AA success criterion setting a minimum size for pointer-input targets | **SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum)** (Level AA, added in WCAG 2.2) |
| 2 | That minimum size | **24 by 24 CSS pixels** (per-side minimum 24) |
| 3 | Diameter of the circle used by its spacing exception | **24 CSS pixel diameter** |
| 4 | Size required by Level AAA 'Target Size (Enhanced)' | **44 by 44 CSS pixels** (per-side minimum 44) — SC 2.5.5 |

## 1. The Level AA criterion: SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum)

WCAG 2.2 Recommendation, Guideline 2.5 Input Modalities:

> **Success Criterion 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum)**
> (Level AA)
> New
> The size of the target for pointer inputs is at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, except when:

Corroborating sources fetched:
- WCAG 2.2 Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/) — normative text above.
- Understanding SC 2.5.8 (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/target-size-minimum.html) — "SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) (Level AA)".
- Quick Reference (https://www.w3.org/WAI/quickref/) — "2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) Level AA (Added in 2.2)".
- What's New in WCAG 2.2 — lists 2.5.8 under "Guideline 2.5 Input Modalities" as a new AA criterion.

Note on disambiguation: SC 2.5.8 is the **AA** criterion and was added in WCAG 2.2. SC 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced) is **AAA** and dates from WCAG 2.1. A third, non-normative WCAG 2.1 AAA-era criterion (2.5.5) is sometimes confused with the AA requirement; only 2.5.8 is the AA minimum-size criterion.

## 2. The minimum size: 24 CSS pixels

Normative wording: "at least **24 by 24 CSS pixels**".

- The per-side minimum is **24 CSS pixels**; the requirement is a floor ("at least"), not a target value or a ceiling.
- The criterion applies to all pointer inputs — mouse, trackpad, pen/stylus, touch — not only touch. The Understanding document is explicit: "this criterion is scoped to all pointer input modalities – not just touch, but also mouse, trackpad, stylus and others."
- Units are **CSS pixels**, which WCAG defines as density-independent and "distinct from actual hardware pixels present in a display". They are not physical pixels, device pixels or points.

## 3. The spacing exception's circle: 24 CSS pixel diameter

Normative wording of the Spacing exception under SC 2.5.8:

> **Spacing**
> Undersized targets (those less than 24 by 24 CSS pixels) are positioned so that if a **24 CSS pixel diameter circle** is centered on the bounding box of each, the circles do not intersect another target or the circle for another undersized target;

Key points for correct application:

- The diameter is **24 CSS pixels** — numerically the same as the base minimum, deliberately so. The circle is *not* required to be larger than the minimum target size; the exception is satisfied by **non-intersection**, not by a larger buffer.
- The circle is centered on the **bounding box** of each undersized target. For square/rectangular targets the circle is effectively centered on the target; for convex and concave shapes it is centered on the bounding box, which may lie outside the visible target (as the Understanding document's Figure 4 illustrates for concave targets).
- The exception only becomes relevant for **undersized** targets, defined in the same sentence as those **less than 24 by 24 CSS pixels**. A target that is 24 by 24 or larger passes on size alone and needs no spacing analysis.
- The test is pairwise: the circle must not intersect (a) another target, or (b) the circle of another undersized target.
- Worked example from the Understanding document: a row of six icon buttons at 20 by 20 CSS pixels with 4 CSS pixels of space between them passes via the spacing exception (20 + 4 + 4 = 28 ≥ 24 across the gap in each direction), whereas the same row at 24 by 24 passes on size without invoking the exception.

## 4. Level AAA 'Target Size (Enhanced)': 44 CSS pixels

WCAG 2.2 Recommendation, SC 2.5.5:

> **Success Criterion 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced)**
> (Level AAA)
> The size of the target for pointer inputs is at least **44 by 44 CSS pixels** except when:
> **Equivalent** — The target is available through an equivalent link or control on the same page that is at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels;
> **Inline** — The target is in a sentence or block of text;
> **User Agent Control** — The size of the target is determined by the user agent and is not modified by the author;
> **Essential** — A particular presentation of the target is essential to the information being conveyed.

So the enhanced per-side minimum is **44 CSS pixels** (44 by 44 CSS pixels).

Important structural difference: **SC 2.5.5 has no spacing exception.** Its exceptions are Equivalent, Inline, User Agent Control and Essential only. The 24-CSS-pixel-diameter circle belongs exclusively to SC 2.5.8 and must not be imported into the AAA criterion.

The two figures are explicitly related in the Understanding document for 2.5.8:

> "…the Working Group settled on the smaller measure of 24 by 24 CSS pixels for the '(Minimum)' version of this criterion, while 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced) uses the larger 44 by 44 CSS pixel measure as its threshold size."

## Consistency check across the four values

- 24 (AA minimum) < 44 (AAA minimum) — consistent with the AA/AAA escalation and with the Understanding document's own comparative statement.
- 24 (spacing circle diameter) = 24 (AA minimum) — intentional, and consistent with the definition of "undersized" as *strictly less than* 24 by 24 CSS pixels; no value in this answer is presented as exceeding a bound it also sets.
- All three numeric values are in **CSS pixels**, matching the normative text verbatim; no conversion to device or physical pixels is made or implied.

## Minimal conformance checklist implied by these values

1. Identify all pointer-input targets in the content.
2. A target ≥ 24 by 24 CSS pixels in both dimensions passes SC 2.5.8 on size.
3. A target < 24 by 24 CSS pixels must satisfy the Spacing exception (24 CSS pixel diameter circles centered on bounding boxes do not intersect any other target or any other undersized target's circle) or another of the five exceptions (Equivalent, Inline, User Agent Control, Essential).
4. To reach AAA for this topic, every target must be ≥ 44 by 44 CSS pixels, or fall under one of SC 2.5.5's four exceptions.

IVs generated using the RBG-based construction
According to section 8.2.2, for IVs generated using the RBG -based construction, the random field (and
hence, the IV itself) must have length r ≥ 96 bits, and for any given IV length, the value r must be fixed for
the life of the key. Thus, for IVs generated using the RBG-based construction and where only one IV length
is allowed per key, one option is to limit the total number of IVs with a given key to 2s, where
s = min((r-31)/2, 48.5).

public class RBGNonce
extends Object
implements Nonce


RBG-based nonce generation strategy that uses a RBG component to produce
 values for the invocation field as described in NIST 
 SP-800-38D, section 8.2.2.

 
NOTE: users of this class are responsible for counting
 number of invocations and enforcing the constraints described in section 8.3;
 namely the following:


 
The total number of invocations of the authenticated encryption
 function shall not exceed 232, including all IV lengths and all
 instances of the authenticated encryption function with the given key.
 


 
Instances of this class are thread safe.

comparison with SP 800-38D bound of 2-32 for the tolerable probability of the (key, IV) pair
collisions. Hence one should only be concerned with the probability of the IV collisions among the
separate encryptions within the same SSHv2 session.
B.  IV generation method
A new IV parameter is generated by the module for each AES-GCM encryption. As shown in Section
7.1 of RFC 5647, the IV consists of a 4-byte fixed field and an 8-byte invocation counter. The initial
IV value is generated as shown in Figure 1 of RFC 5647 and the fixed field of this IV remains the
same for the duration of the session. Therefore, the method for minimizing the (key, IV) collision
probability within the same session depends entirely on the management of the invocation field of the
IV. The invocation counter is treated as a 64-bit integer and is incremented by one when performing
an AES-GCM encryption of a new binary packet. The formation of binary packets is explained in
Section 7.2 of RFC 5647.
C.  A Method of Compliance
If an IV is constructed in compliance with the SSHv2 protocol, then this IV shall only be used in the
context of the AES-GCM mode encryptions within the SSHv2 protocol.

2. Questions on wGCM:
Would a limit of 264 wGCM invocations per key be sufficient?
What authentication tag sizes should be specified for wGCM (e.g., 128, 192, or 256 bits) to support larger data limits than GCM? Is more than one tag size necessary?
NIST proposes 192 bits as the default IV length for wGCM, devoting the remaining 64 bits of the IV block within wGCM to the message block counter for the GCTR encryption. Is there a need to support longer IVs in wGCM by applying the internal hash function, as in GCM?
The deterministic IV construction for GCM defines a fixed field and an invocation field. For wGCM, NIST proposes to recommend a fixed field of 96 bits and an invocation field of 96 bits to promote interoperability. Are other options needed?
The random IV construction for GCM defines a random field and a free field. For wGCM, if the number of invocations per key were limited to 264, and if 192 bits were specified for the random field, then the probability of an IV collision would be limited to 2-64.  Is the free field useful/necessary for wGCM?
Are these two 192-bit IV constructions sufficiently flexible, or should NIST consider adding other, comparably secure constructions?

The natural generalization of the GCM hash function (i.e., GHASH) for wGCM would specify a suitable polynomial of degree 256 to define a hash function (called wide-GHASH) on 256-bit blocks. The output can be truncated as needed to obtain the appropriate tag size. Should NIST consider a different option for the hash function component of wGCM? For example, two instances of GHASH using independent 128-bit keys could be concatenated and truncated as needed. Since this option (called concat-GHASH) operates on 128-bit blocks, it would be more efficient than wide-GHASH. However, concat-GHASH cannot provide as much generic security assurance as wide-GHASH and would require much more restrictive usage bounds (i.e., smaller limits on total data, the message length, and invocations per key) for any given security target.

verdict.summary:
Scope: NIST SP 800-38D, November 2007 edition, AES-GCM, IVs generated by the RBG-based construction in §8.2.2.

1. IV length to restrict support to: 96 bits (12 bytes).

SP 800-38D §8.2.2 defines the RBG-based IV as the concatenation of a random field and a free field. The random field shall be at least 96 bits; the free field may be empty. For a 96-bit IV, the random field is the entire IV and the free field is empty. SP 800-38D §5.2.1.1 identifies 96 bits as the recommended/default IV length. The standard does not absolutely forbid longer IVs under the RBG-based construction (the random field may be ≥96 bits with a nonempty free field), but 96 bits is the length implementations should restrict support to for interoperability and to avoid the non-96-bit GHASH-based IV derivation. If multiple IV lengths are supported, the lengths and field boundaries shall be fixed for the life of the key; any supported IV length strictly less than 96 bits must use the deterministic construction in §8.2.1, not the RBG-based construction.

2. Maximum total number of authenticated-encryption invocations under one key: 2^32 = 4,294,967,296 invocations.

SP 800-38D §8.3 states that the total number of invocations of the authenticated encryption function shall not exceed 2^32, including all IV lengths and all instances of the authenticated encryption function with the given key. This requirement applies because the RBG-based construction is in use; it is not waived by using 96-bit IVs, since the waiver applies only when an implementation uses exclusively 96-bit IVs generated by the deterministic construction. The limit is global per key and must be enforced by appropriate local counters across all instances. It applies to authenticated encryption; authenticated decryption has separate limits in Appendix C and is not the same quantity.

3. Maximum plaintext length per invocation: 2^39 − 256 bits = 2^36 − 32 bytes = 68,719,476,704 bytes (approximately 64 GiB minus 32 bytes).

SP 800-38D §5.2.1.1 limits the plaintext length to at most 2^39 − 256 bits. Conversion:

(2^39 − 256) / 8 = 2^36 − 32 = 68,719,476,704 bytes.

Check: 68,719,476,704 bytes × 8 = 549,755,813,632 bits = 2^39 − 256 bits. The ciphertext has the same maximum length. The AAD maximum is separate (2^64 − 1 bits), and tag length does not alter the plaintext maximum.

quotes.whole:
By default, initdb uses the locale provider libc (see Section 23.1.4). The libc locale provider takes the locale settings from the environment, and determines the encoding from the locale settings.
To choose a different locale for the cluster, use the option --locale. There are also individual options --lc-* and --icu-locale (see below) to set values for the individual locale categories. Note that inconsistent settings for different locale categories can give nonsensical results, so this should be used with care.
Alternatively, initdb can use the ICU library to provide locale services by specifying --locale-provider=icu. The server must be built with ICU support. To choose the specific ICU locale ID to apply, use the option --icu-locale. Note that for implementation reasons and to support legacy code, initdb will still select and initialize libc locale settings when the ICU locale provider is used.
When initdb runs, it will print out the locale settings it has chosen. If you have complex requirements or specified multiple options, it is advisable to check that the result matches what was intended.
More details about locale settings can be found in Section 23.1.

quotes.whole:
28.2.1. Off-line Enabling of Checksums
By default, data pages are protected by checksums, but this can optionally be disabled for a cluster. When enabled, each data page includes a checksum that is updated when the page is written and verified each time the page is read. Only data pages are protected by checksums; internal data structures and temporary files are not.
Checksums can be disabled when the cluster is initialized using initdb. They can also be enabled or disabled at a later time as an offline operation. Data checksums are enabled or disabled at the full cluster level, and cannot be specified individually for databases or tables.
The current state of checksums in the cluster can be verified by viewing the value of the read-only configuration variable data_checksums by issuing the command SHOW data_checksums.
When attempting to recover from page corruptions, it may be necessary to bypass the checksum protection. To do this, temporarily set the configuration parameter ignore_checksum_failure.
28.2.1. Off-line Enabling of Checksums #
The pg_checksums application can be used to enable or disable data checksums, as well as verify checksums, on an offline cluster.

If you have already migrated the cluster to a platform with different char signedness (for example, from an x86-based system to an ARM-based system), you should use this option to specify the signedness matching the original platform's default char signedness. Additionally, it's essential not to modify any data files between migrating data files and running pg_upgrade. pg_upgrade should be the first operation that starts the cluster on the new platform.
--swap
Move the data directories from the old cluster to the new cluster. Then, replace the catalog files with those generated for the new cluster. This mode can outperform --link, --clone, --copy, and --copy-file-range, especially on clusters with many relations.
However, this mode creates many garbage files in the old cluster, which can prolong the file synchronization step if --sync-method=syncfs is used. Therefore, it is recommended to use --sync-method=fsync with --swap.
Additionally, once the file transfer step begins, the old cluster will be destructively modified and therefore will no longer be safe to start. See Step 17 for details.

quotes.whole:
Reverting to old cluster
If, after running pg_upgrade, you wish to revert to the old cluster, there are several options:
If the --check option was used, the old cluster was unmodified; it can be restarted.
If neither --link nor --swap was used, the old cluster was unmodified; it can be restarted.
If the --link option was used, the data files might be shared between the old and new cluster:
If pg_upgrade aborted before linking started, the old cluster was unmodified; it can be restarted.
If you did not start the new cluster, the old cluster was unmodified except that, when linking started, a .old suffix was appended to $PGDATA/global/pg_control. To reuse the old cluster, remove the .old suffix from $PGDATA/global/pg_control; you can then restart the old cluster.
If you did start the new cluster, it has written to shared files and it is unsafe to use the old cluster. The old cluster will need to be restored from backup in this case.
If the --swap option was used, the old cluster might be destructively modified:
If pg_upgrade aborts before reporting that the old cluster is no longer safe to start, the old cluster was unmodified; it can be restarted.

quotes.whole:
By default, initdb uses the locale provider libc (see Section 23.1.4). The libc locale provider takes the locale settings from the environment, and determines the encoding from the locale settings.
To choose a different locale for the cluster, use the option --locale. There are also individual options --lc-* and --icu-locale (see below) to set values for the individual locale categories. Note that inconsistent settings for different locale categories can give nonsensical results, so this should be used with care.
Alternatively, initdb can use the ICU library to provide locale services by specifying --locale-provider=icu. The server must be built with ICU support. To choose the specific ICU locale ID to apply, use the option --icu-locale. Note that for implementation reasons and to support legacy code, initdb will still select and initialize libc locale settings when the ICU locale provider is used.
When initdb runs, it will print out the locale settings it has chosen. If you have complex requirements or specified multiple options, it is advisable to check that the result matches what was intended.
More details about locale settings can be found in Section 23.1.

quotes.whole:
28.2.1. Off-line Enabling of Checksums
By default, data pages are protected by checksums, but this can optionally be disabled for a cluster. When enabled, each data page includes a checksum that is updated when the page is written and verified each time the page is read. Only data pages are protected by checksums; internal data structures and temporary files are not.
Checksums can be disabled when the cluster is initialized using initdb. They can also be enabled or disabled at a later time as an offline operation. Data checksums are enabled or disabled at the full cluster level, and cannot be specified individually for databases or tables.
The current state of checksums in the cluster can be verified by viewing the value of the read-only configuration variable data_checksums by issuing the command SHOW data_checksums.
When attempting to recover from page corruptions, it may be necessary to bypass the checksum protection. To do this, temporarily set the configuration parameter ignore_checksum_failure.
28.2.1. Off-line Enabling of Checksums #
The pg_checksums application can be used to enable or disable data checksums, as well as verify checksums, on an offline cluster.

verdict.summary:
# PostgreSQL 18 data checksums: default, disabling, and pg_upgrade constraint

## 1. Verdict — yes, data checksums are enabled

In PostgreSQL 18, `initdb` enables data page checksums by default. A cluster created with

```
initdb -D /var/lib/pgsql/18/data
```

(passing no `--data-checksums` / `--no-data-checksums` / `-k` option) **has data checksums enabled**. There is no checksum-related prompt or warning; the setting is silent.

Grounding (PostgreSQL 18 docs):

- `initdb` reference, `-k / --data-checksums`: *"Use checksums on data pages to help detect corruption by the I/O system that would otherwise be silent. **This is enabled by default; use --no-data-checksums to disable checksums.**"*
- Chapter 28.2 (Checksums): *"**By default, data pages are protected by checksums**, but this can optionally be disabled for a cluster."*
- Release 18, incompatibilities: *"Change initdb default to enable data checksums (Greg Sabino Mullane). Checksums can be disabled with the new initdb option --no-data-checksums. pg_upgrade requires matching cluster checksum settings, so this new option can be useful to upgrade non-checksum old clusters."*

**Version caveat that matters operationally:** this default flipped in 18. In PostgreSQL 17 and earlier the default was *off* and `-k/--data-checksums` was required to turn it on. So `initdb` with no flags now produces a materially different cluster than it did on 17, and any runbook, automation, or Ansible/Terraform module written for <=17 that relied on the implicit "no checksums" default is now wrong.

### Verifying the state (do this, don't assume)

```
-- server running:
SHOW data_checksums;          -- 'on' or 'off'

-- server stopped (authoritative, from the control file):
pg_controldata -D /var/lib/pgsql/18/data | grep -i checksum
#   Data page checksum version:           1     -> enabled
#   Data page checksum version:           0     -> disabled
```

`data_checksums` is a read-only, informational GUC (`GUC_DISALLOW_IN_FILE`): it cannot be set in `postgresql.conf`, cannot be set via `ALTER SYSTEM`, and cannot be changed with `SET`. Attempting to put it in `postgresql.conf` prevents startup. Checksums are a **cluster-wide, on-disk property**, not a per-database or per-table setting, and there is **no online toggle**.

Do not confuse two adjacent things:
- `ignore_checksum_failure` (a real, settable GUC) only makes the server *log and continue* on a bad checksum during recovery/reads. It does **not** disable checksum storage or verification.
- `wal_log_hints` / `full_page_writes` are unrelated to whether data pages carry checksums.

## 2. How checksums are switched off

There are exactly two supported mechanisms; both are offline in the sense that they act on stored pages, not on a running server's configuration.

### 2a. At cluster creation (the normal answer, and the one you want for a fresh PG18 cluster)

```
initdb -D /var/lib/pgsql/18/data --no-data-checksums
```

`--no-data-checksums` is **new in PostgreSQL 18** (it did not exist before, because "off" was the default). `-k/--data-checksums` still exists as an explicit (now redundant) enable. For scripted installs, pass the flag explicitly rather than relying on the default of whichever `initdb` binary is on `PATH` — that makes the cluster's checksum state deterministic across PG17 and PG18 tooling.

### 2b. On an existing cluster — `pg_checksums` (offline, server must be stopped)

```
# 1. Clean shutdown is mandatory — pg_checksums refuses a cluster that is not cleanly shut down.
pg_ctl -D /var/lib/pgsql/18/data stop -m fast

# 2. Disable checksums, rewriting every data page in the cluster.
pg_checksums -D /var/lib/pgsql/18/data --disable --progress --verbose

# 3. Confirm, then restart.
pg_controldata -D /var/lib/pgsql/18/data | grep -i checksum   # -> version 0
pg_ctl -D /var/lib/pgsql/18/data start
```

`pg_checksums` can `--enable`, `--disable`, or `--check` (verify only) at the whole-cluster level. Same tool, inverse flag: `pg_checksums -D $PGDATA --enable`.

Operational rules for 2b:
- **Downtime is required and proportional to cluster size.** `--disable` rewrites every heap/index page; on a multi-hundred-GB cluster this is a maintenance-window operation, not a config flip.
- **The cluster must be cleanly shut down** (no crash-in-progress, no immediate shutdown leaving it unrecovered). Otherwise the tool aborts.
- **It cannot run against a running server, and it does not stream to standbys.** After the operation, every physical standby is out of sync with the primary's page contents — take a fresh base backup and rebuild standbys (`pg_basebackup`), and invalidate incremental/`pg_rewind` expectations. Do not attempt this on a primary that has live replicas without planning for that rebuild.
- **Idempotence:** running `--disable` on a cluster already at version 0 (or `--enable` on one already at 1) reports that state and exits without rewriting; it is safe but pointless.
- **No config-file alternative exists.** There is no `postgresql.conf`/`ALTER SYSTEM` path; anything claiming otherwise is wrong for 18.

### 2c. What is *not* a way to switch checksums off

- `ALTER SYSTEM SET data_checksums = off;` — rejected; the GUC is not settable.
- `SET ignore_checksum_failure = on;` — suppresses the error, does not remove checksums.
- Recreating individual databases/tables — checksums are cluster-level only.
- `pg_dump`/`pg_restore` — data-only logical operations never change the cluster's checksum version.

## 3. Constraint for `pg_upgrade` — checksum settings must match

**The old cluster and the new cluster must have the same data-checksum setting.** `pg_upgrade` reads both clusters' `pg_controldata` and aborts if the *Data page checksum version* differs (`0` vs `1`), because the upgrade transfers data files physically (`--link`, `--clone`, `--copy`, `--copy-file-range`, `--swap`) rather than re-writing pages logically; the new server would otherwise interpret every page under the wrong checksum convention. This is a hard preflight failure, not a warning.

Consequences, stated as a decision matrix (old cluster → how you must initialize the new one):

| Old cluster (source) checksums | Required new-cluster `initdb` | `pg_upgrade` outcome |
|---|---|---|
| off (version 0) — typical PG<=17 cluster | `initdb ... --no-data-checksums` | succeeds |
| off (version 0) | `initdb ...` (PG18 default, on) | **fails preflight** — checksum version mismatch |
| on (version 1) | `initdb ...` (PG18 default, on) | succeeds |
| on (version 1) | `initdb ... --no-data-checksums` | **fails preflight** — checksum version mismatch |

This is precisely why the release notes pair the two facts: *"pg_upgrade requires matching cluster checksum settings, so this new option can be useful to upgrade non-checksum old clusters."* The overwhelmingly common case in 2026 — upgrading a pre-18 cluster that was initialized without `-k` — now needs `--no-data-checksums` on the new cluster, or the upgrade dies in preflight.

### Procedure

1. **Determine the old cluster's state before touching anything:**
   ```
   pg_controldata -D /old/pgdata | grep -i 'checksum'
   ```
   (`0` = off, `1` = on.)
2. **Initialize the new PG18 cluster with the matching flag:**
   ```
   # old cluster off:
   initdb -D /new/pgdata --no-data-checksums
   # old cluster on:
   initdb -D /new/pgdata            # default is on in 18; --data-checksums also valid
   ```
   Also keep the other compatibility-relevant `initdb` choices aligned with the old cluster (locale provider/locale, encoding, `--set-char-signedness` considerations for pre-18 sources), since `pg_upgrade` validates more than checksums.
3. **Run the preflight first, in the same shape as the real run:**
   ```
   pg_upgrade --check \
     -b /usr/pgsql-18/bin -B /usr/pgsql-18/bin \
     -d /old/pgdata -D /new/pgdata
   ```
   `--check` performs the same `pg_controldata` comparison, so a checksum mismatch surfaces here (cheaply) instead of mid-window. Never skip this.
4. **Run the upgrade**, then follow the standard post-upgrade steps (analyze, delete old cluster after verification).

### If the settings already mismatch, the three remedies

- **Re-initdb the new cluster with the right flag** (cleanest; do it before the window — the new cluster is empty, so it costs seconds).
- **`pg_checksums --disable` on the freshly initialized, still-empty new cluster** — near-instant on an empty cluster, and legitimate because the cluster is stopped and cleanly shut down. Equivalent outcome to `--no-data-checksums`, useful when the installer already ran `initdb` for you.
- **`pg_checksums --enable` on the old cluster before upgrading** — only if you *want* to land on checksums-on. This requires full downtime on the old production cluster (every page rewritten), plus a fresh base backup and standby rebuild afterwards, so it is usually the wrong trade unless you also wanted checksums enabled as an end state.

Do **not** try to work around the mismatch by editing `pg_controldata` output, copying `pg_control`, or hand-patching the new cluster: the checksum version is baked into the page headers, and a forged control file yields a cluster that fails verification on first read.

## 4. One-paragraph answer for the DBA

In PostgreSQL 18 a bare `initdb` produces a cluster **with data checksums enabled** (this is a change from 17 and earlier, where the default was off). Checksums are switched off either at creation with the new `initdb --no-data-checksums` option, or offline on an existing cluster with `pg_checksums -D $PGDATA --disable` after a clean shutdown — there is no online or configuration-file switch, `data_checksums` being a read-only GUC, and the offline path rewrites every page, so plan downtime, take a new base backup, and rebuild standbys afterwards. When running `pg_upgrade`, the **old and new clusters must have identical checksum settings**; `pg_upgrade` compares `pg_controldata` and refuses to proceed otherwise, so an old non-checksum cluster must be paired with a new cluster created via `initdb --no-data-checksums` (or a `pg_checksums --disable` on the empty new cluster) — verify both sides with `pg_controldata | grep -i checksum` and confirm with `pg_upgrade --check` before the maintenance window.

Version Skew Policy
The maximum version skew supported between various Kubernetes components.
This document describes the maximum version skew supported between various Kubernetes components.
Specific cluster deployment tools may place additional restrictions on version skew.
Supported versions
Kubernetes versions are expressed as x.y.z, where x is the major version,
y is the minor version, and z is the patch version, following
Semantic Versioning terminology. For more information, see
Kubernetes Release Versioning.
The Kubernetes project maintains release branches for the most recent three minor releases
(1.37, 1.36, 1.35).
Kubernetes 1.19 and newer receive approximately 1 year of patch support.
Kubernetes 1.18 and older received approximately 9 months of patch support.

kubeadm upgrade does not touch your workloads, only components internal to Kubernetes, but backups are always a best practice.

Upgrades & Version Skew
Keeping Kubernetes clusters up-to-date is essential for security, new features, and bug fixes. However, upgrading a Kubernetes cluster requires careful planning because different components can run different versions—a concept called “version skew.” Understanding version skew policies and upgrade strategies ensures upgrades happen safely without breaking running applications.
Think of upgrading Kubernetes like renovating a building while people are still working inside. You need to upgrade components in the right order, ensure compatibility between old and new versions, and minimize disruption to ongoing operations.
Why Upgrade?

verdict.summary:
# Verdict

Given a **kube-apiserver at v1.27**, of the three candidates **only kubelet v1.25 is inside the supported skew**.

| kubelet | Δ (apiserver minor − kubelet minor) | Newer than apiserver? | Applicable max downward skew | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| v1.28 | −1 (newer) | **yes** | 0 (kubelet may never be newer) | **OUTSIDE** |
| v1.25 | 2 | no | 3 (general rule; 25 ≥ 25 so carve-out does not apply) | **INSIDE** |
| v1.24 | 3 | no | 2 (kubelet < 1.25 carve-out) | **OUTSIDE** |

Supported kubelet window for a v1.27 kube-apiserver: **{v1.27, v1.26, v1.25}** — i.e. `27 − 3 = 24` is the naive floor, but v1.24 is excluded by the carve-out, so the effective floor is v1.25.

---

## 1. Governing policy text (as fetched, quoted verbatim)

Source: https://kubernetes.io/releases/version-skew-policy/index.html (sha256 12c9be324268)

> "kubelet
> kubelet must not be newer than kube-apiserver.
> kubelet may be up to three minor versions older than kube-apiserver (kubelet < 1.25 may only be up to two minor versions older than kube-apiserver).
> Example:
> kube-apiserver is at 1.37
> kubelet is supported at 1.37, 1.36, 1.35, and 1.34"

Source: https://referencesource.org/kubernetes-version-skew-policy/ (sha256 f3e436cff138) — restates the same rule in tabular form:

> "kube-apiserver and kubelet | kubelet may be up to three minor versions older than kube-apiserver | Max skew (minor versions): 3 | May the second component be newer? no | ... | Exception for older versions: kubelet < 1.25 may only be up to two minor versions older than kube-apiserver"

Three clauses are load-bearing:

1. **Direction is one-way.** The kubelet may never be newer than the kube-apiserver — not by one minor, not by one patch-within-a-newer-minor. This alone disqualifies v1.28.
2. **Downward allowance is counted in whole minors, inclusive of the apiserver's own minor.** The worked example (1.37 → 1.37, 1.36, 1.35, 1.34) enumerates four versions = the apiserver's minor plus three older minors. So the bound is `apiserver_minor − kubelet_minor ≤ 3`, not `< 3` and not `≤ 2`.
3. **The carve-out is a property of the kubelet's minor, not the apiserver's.** The subject of "kubelet < 1.25" is the kubelet. A kubelet at minor < 25 gets a maximum downward skew of **2**, regardless of how new the apiserver is. v1.24 is the first version caught by this.

## 2. Per-candidate derivation

**kubelet v1.28 — OUTSIDE.** It is one minor *newer* than the v1.27 apiserver. The "must not be newer" clause is absolute and has no patch-level escape hatch; a v1.28.0 kubelet against a v1.27.x apiserver is out of policy, as is v1.28.x against v1.27.y for any x, y. No downward-skew allowance can rescue a newer kubelet, so the carve-out and the 3-minor allowance are irrelevant here.

**kubelet v1.25 — INSIDE.** Δ = 27 − 25 = 2. It is older, so clause 1 is satisfied. kubelet minor 25 is **not** `< 25`, so the general allowance of 3 applies: 2 ≤ 3 → supported. (It is also ≤ the older 2-minor bound — see §4.)

**kubelet v1.24 — OUTSIDE.** Δ = 27 − 24 = 3. It is older, so clause 1 is satisfied, and 3 ≤ 3 would pass the *general* rule. But kubelet minor 24 **is** `< 25`, so the carve-out caps the allowance at 2: 3 > 2 → **not supported**. This is exactly the off-by-one trap: applying the 3-minor rule without the parenthetical wrongly admits v1.24.

## 3. What the answer does *not* depend on

- **Patch versions.** Skew is defined at the minor level ("Kubernetes versions are expressed as x.y.z ... y is the minor version"). kubelet v1.25.16 against kube-apiserver v1.27.8 is in policy exactly as v1.25.0 against v1.27.0 would be. No patch pairing changes any verdict above.
- **Counting convention.** I verified the boundary by enumerating rather than by subtracting: {1.27, 1.26, 1.25, 1.24} is the 4-version set the general rule would produce, matching the 1.37 example's 4-version set; the carve-out then truncates the oldest member.

## 4. Robustness across policy eras (why the verdict is era-invariant)

The request's framing ("kube-apiserver at v1.27") implies the v1.27-era policy text, which predates the extension to three minors. A third-party source in the evidence base still states the older wording:

> https://k8s.guru/docs/cluster-ops/upgrades/ (sha256 58b2d96e897b): "kubelet can be up to 2 minor versions older than kube-apiserver"

I therefore evaluated all three candidates under **both** rule sets:

| kubelet | Δ | Old rule (max 2, no carve-out) | Current rule (max 3; max 2 if kubelet < 1.25) | Agreement? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| v1.28 | −1 | OUT (newer) | OUT (newer) | yes |
| v1.25 | 2 | 2 ≤ 2 → IN | 2 ≤ 3 → IN | yes |
| v1.24 | 3 | 3 > 2 → OUT | 3 > 2 (carve-out) → OUT | yes |

**All three verdicts are identical under both eras**, so the answer is not sensitive to which policy revision the question intends. The two eras first diverge at a combination *not* asked here — (apiserver v1.28, kubelet v1.25): current rule admits it (Δ = 3, kubelet 25 not < 25), the old 2-minor rule rejects it. Flagging this so nobody generalises the v1.27 answer forward past the next apiserver minor without re-running the check.

## 5. Reference implementation (drop-in CI check)

```python
# skew.py — kubelet-vs-apiserver skew check, current policy text.
# Usage: kubelet_supported(apiserver_minor=27, kubelet_minor=25) -> (bool, reason)

def kubelet_supported(apiserver_minor: int, kubelet_minor: int) -> tuple[bool, str]:
    """Return (supported, reason) for a kubelet against a kube-apiserver,
    evaluated at the minor-version level per the Kubernetes version skew policy.

    Policy (kubernetes.io/releases/version-skew-policy):
      - kubelet must not be newer than kube-apiserver            (max upward skew = 0)
      - kubelet may be up to 3 minors older than kube-apiserver
      - exception: kubelet < 1.25 may be at most 2 minors older
    """
    if kubelet_minor > apiserver_minor:
        return False, (
            f"kubelet 1.{kubelet_minor} is newer than kube-apiserver 1.{apiserver_minor}; "
            "the kubelet must never be newer (allowed upward skew = 0)"
        )

    delta = apiserver_minor - kubelet_minor
    if kubelet_minor < 25:
        max_skew, rule = 2, "kubelet < 1.25 carve-out (max 2 minors older)"
    else:
        max_skew, rule = 3, "general rule (max 3 minors older)"

    supported = delta <= max_skew
    return supported, (
        f"kubelet 1.{kubelet_minor} vs kube-apiserver 1.{apiserver_minor}: "
        f"delta={delta}, max_skew={max_skew} [{rule}] -> "
        f"{'SUPPORTED' if supported else 'NOT SUPPORTED'}"
    )
```

Test vectors (all must pass; the last two pin the off-by-one and the carve-out):

```python
cases = [
    ((27, 28), False),  # newer than apiserver
    ((27, 27), True),   # delta 0
    ((27, 26), True),   # delta 1
    ((27, 25), True),   # delta 2  <- asked, INSIDE
    ((27, 24), False),  # delta 3 but kubelet < 1.25 -> cap 2  <- asked, OUTSIDE
    ((28, 25), True),   # delta 3, kubelet 25 -> allowed (era-divergent case)
    ((26, 24), True),   # delta 2, kubelet < 1.25 -> cap 2, exactly at bound
]
for (api, kl), expected in cases:
    got, why = kubelet_supported(api, kl)
    assert got is expected, (api, kl, expected, why)
```

Shell one-liner to read the live values from a cluster before applying this logic:

```bash
kubectl version -o json | jq -r '.serverVersion.minor'   # apiserver minor, e.g. "27"
kubectl get nodes -o json | jq -r '.items[].status.nodeInfo.kubeletVersion'  # e.g. v1.28.3, v1.25.16, v1.24.17
```

(Strip any `+`/`-`/vendor suffix from the minor field, e.g. `27+`, before integer comparison — managed offerings often return suffixed minors.)

## 6. Assumptions and scope notes

- **Single apiserver at v1.27.** If the cluster is HA with instances spanning two minors (e.g. v1.27 and v1.26), the policy narrows the window to the *oldest* apiserver instance: kubelet v1.27 would fall out (newer than the v1.26 instance) while v1.25 remains in (within 2 minors of both 1.27 and 1.26). The question states a single v1.27 apiserver, so this does not change the verdict.
- **No vendor/tool-added restrictions.** "Specific cluster deployment tools may place additional restrictions on version skew" — EKS/GKE/AKS and some kubeadm configurations narrow this further. The verdict above is the upstream Kubernetes policy only.
- **"Inside the supported skew" ≠ "still a supported release."** v1.25 is skew-compliant against a v1.27 apiserver but is itself past its patch-support window; skew compliance is a compatibility statement, not a maintenance statement.
- **Out-of-skew ≠ broken.** v1.24 and v1.28 kubelets may well register and function against a v1.27 apiserver; the policy statement is about what is tested and guaranteed, not about observed behaviour.
- **kube-proxy not in scope.** It has its own (currently identical) rule and is not part of this ask.

## 7. Operational consequence (upgrade-order implication)

Because the kubelet may lag but never lead: **upgrade the kube-apiserver first, then the kubelets**, one minor at a time. Concretely, from a v1.27 apiserver with a v1.24 kubelet in the fleet, the remediation is to bring that kubelet to **at least v1.25 before** the apiserver advances (or immediately, if the apiserver is already at v1.27), since v1.24 is already out of policy against v1.27 today. Any kubelet pinned at v1.28 must be rolled back to ≤ v1.27 or the apiserver advanced to v1.28 in the same change window.
